gaps.category: Federal Tax Authority duties for micro-businesses: VAT registration and quarterly returns, Corporate Tax (9% from 2023, small business relief ending 31 Dec 2026), mandatory registration of exempt persons and free-zone entities, and the Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax

General accounting tools are out of scope, but a narrowly defined duty such as the end of small business relief, or the CT return for free-zone qualifying persons, may qualify.

gaps.why: Dubai's trading economy has a very large number of micro-importers and re-exporters (Deira, Karama, Sharjah). result.competitor: No scrap-specific product was found in Arabic or English searches. Zoho Books has a generic "Enable Reverse Charge in Sales Transactions" setting, and its UAE reverse-charge guides cover imports. None mention scrap or a declaration workflow. No release notes were found from Wafeq, Daftra, Tally or Focus. However, the core job is thin. The invoice statement and 0%/RC tax code can be set up in any UAE accounting tool, which already did this for the earlier RCM on gold and electronics. A stored declaration is a PDF attachment, and TRN verification can be done with the FTA's free online TRN check. Advisory firms (PwC, KPMG, Crowe, AJMS, Bestaxca) cover the advice side. The gap is a niche feature, not a product.
result.duty: The duty is real and in force. Cabinet Decision No. 153 of 2025 was published in the Official Gazette on 26 Nov 2025. It applies to supplies on or after 14 Jan 2026, and the UAE legislation portal lists it as Active with effective date 13 Jan 2026. It covers local supplies of metal scrap between VAT-registered parties where the buyer will resell or process the scrap; zero-rated supplies are excluded. Before the supply date the buyer must give written declarations covering its purpose and its FTA registration. The supplier must keep those declarations, verify the buyer's registration by an FTA-approved method, and state on the invoice that reverse charge applies. If the conditions fail, the supplier accounts for 5% VAT and the buyer cannot recover the input tax under Art. 54(1)(a)/(b). Frequency: every transaction plus the VAT return, which is usually quarterly. No penalty schedule specific to the decision was found (Gulf News says MoF gave no penalty detail), so the general VAT administrative penalties presumably apply; that is unverified. VATP047 is reported only by a third-party tracker (lookuptax, "medium confidence"), listed as new on the FTA guides page in Oct 2026. Its text was not reached, so it is unverified whether declarations must be given per supply or can be standing.
result.market: Not found. There is no register or statistic of UAE scrap-trading licences or of VAT-registered scrap dealers. The only figure found is about 40.5k commercial licences in Sharjah across all activities (Al Bayan PDF, end 2024), which is not scrap-specific. The UAE is reported to be among the top 10 ferrous scrap exporters, but exports are zero-rated and out of scope. The addressable number of VAT-registered domestic B2B scrap traders is likely in the hundreds to low thousands; this is an estimate and unverified.
result.reason: The duty is real, mandatory and applies to every transaction since 14 Jan 2026, and no scrap-specific tool exists. But the core job is a declaration form, a TRN lookup on the free FTA tool, and fixed invoice wording. Existing UAE accounting tools (Zoho, Odoo, Tally, Wafeq) already handle reverse-charge tax codes and attachments from the gold and electronics RCMs. The buyer group is small and often informal: many collectors are not VAT-registered and so are out of scope. Willingness to pay for a standalone kit is low; accountants would do this with a template. The best route is a free template or ERP add-on sold through accounting firms. Market size, VATP047 details and the penalty schedule could not be verified.

result.competitor: I found no UAE-specific or MoHRE-aligned tool that tracks refund and probation deadlines. Daftra sells a generic, Gulf-wide recruitment-office module covering worker and client tracking, external agencies and accounting, but there is no sign it calculates refunds or deadlines under UAE rules. Qoyod only has a blog post on the topic. The SGC Recruitment Odoo module is built for employers hiring staff, not placement agencies. Generic recruitment CRMs (Recruitly, iSmartRecruit, Bullhorn) and maid-cleaning software (Capterra listings) don't do the core job. I found no MoHRE system that offices must use to track refunds; employers report problems through MoHRE channels (80084 / 600590000). I did not check whether larger offices run in-house ERP; marked not_reached.
result.duty: The duty is real and in force. Under Decree-Law 9/2022 and its executive regulations (Cabinet Resolution 106/2022), licensed domestic-worker recruitment offices must refund recruitment fees within two weeks of a worker being returned or reported absent. The refund is in full during the six-month probation for medical unfitness, absconding or misconduct. In other cases it is pro rata: cost ÷ contract months × remaining months, for example AED 9,000 of AED 12,000 on a 24-month contract left after 6 months. The office also pays repatriation for agency-recruited workers. Penalties: the Schedule 2 fine for a late refund is reported as AED 2,000 per case, from a search snippet, not the full text. Enforcement figures: 300 violations by 57 offices in 2025, mostly late refunds (MoHRE, Feb 2026). In H1 2026, 135 fines went to 42 offices, 106 of them refund cases (WAM, July 2026). Repeat offenders risk licence cancellation. The duty recurs with every placement or return.
result.market: This is a small market. Gulf News (Dec 2025) reports 311 approved offices, but its category counts add up to 325: 136 recruitment centres, 175 business service centres and 14 delivery providers. Only the roughly 136 recruitment centres carry the refund duty. One Arabic source gave about 130 accredited offices (undated), and an Aletihad headline mentions 114 accredited centres. So the realistic buyer pool is about 115–140 offices nationwide. I did not reach a current 2026 count after closures.
result.reason: The duty is mandatory, recurs with each placement, is clearly enforced (late refunds are the most common fine) and creates real pain over deadlines and pro-rata calculations. I found no MoHRE-aligned tool for it. But the buyer pool is tiny, about 115–140 licensed recruitment centres, so even full adoption gives a small revenue ceiling for a solo founder. Refund tracking is a narrow feature, and generic Gulf recruitment-office ERPs such as Daftra could add it easily. Offices fined mostly for not refunding employers may be unwilling, not unable, to pay, which weakens the case that software fixes the problem. Arabic and English interfaces would be needed. A one-off rules calculator is simple to build, but the market size caps the score.

result.competitor: Vet practice management software in the UAE: VetlinkPro (offices in Dubai and Riyadh, Arabic support, per its zoftwarehub listing), Provet Cloud, ezyVet, and other tools listed on Capterra UAE (VETbuddy, VetO, VetMaster). These cover prescriptions, inventory and dispensing records, but I did not confirm a feature built for Decree-Law 21/2025. Tatmeen, the state's track-and-trace platform for human pharmaceuticals, exists, but I could not confirm that it covers veterinary products. I found no vet-specific EDE e-prescription platform.
result.duty: Federal Decree-Law 21/2025 is in force from 1 Jan 2026, with up to 1 year to regularise, extendable by the Cabinet. Requirements: EDE and MOCCAE licensing after local approval; inspections by EDE, MOCCAE and the local authority; only licensed vets may issue or change prescriptions; antibiotics need a prescription and may not be used for prevention or growth promotion; counterfeit, expired and grey-market products are banned; establishments must join the national pharmacovigilance system; national databases are unified. Not found: record-keeping detail, a mandated clinic e-system, and fine amounts (the article only mentions disciplinary and deterrent penalties). The executive regulations were not reached because the uaelegislation.gov.ae and LEAP texts both returned 403.
result.market: Secondary estimates only: about 185 licensed vet hospitals and clinics in 2022 (Ken Research), more than 200 in 2023 (WiFi Talents), and about 400 MOCCAE-licensed clinics (uaefreezonefinder, low reliability). Separately, one source reports about 1,200 licensed vets. EDE carried out 2,030 inspections across the pharmaceutical, agricultural and veterinary sectors in H1 2026 (search summary of WAM; the page fetch returned no content). I found no official register count for vet pharmacies or warehouses.
result.reason: The law is real and in force. Federal Decree-Law 21/2025 took effect on 1 Jan 2026 and gives establishments one year to comply, which the Cabinet can extend. It requires EDE/MOCCAE licensing and inspections, says only licensed vets may issue or change prescriptions, bars antibiotics without a prescription, and requires taking part in pharmacovigilance. However, no source I could reach defines specific record-keeping duties, a mandatory e-system or fine amounts; the official text returned HTTP 403. So the "core job" can't be pinned down yet. Vet practice management software that handles prescriptions and inventory is already sold in the region, for example VetlinkPro with GCC offices and Arabic, plus Provet and ezyVet. The market is tiny, roughly 185 to 400 clinics, and the counts conflict. Pain and willingness to pay are unclear.

result.competitor: Free state tool: the law sets up a unified 'Digital Window' platform (Art. 2 and 8). Owners apply through it and name their engineering firm, and engineering firms submit Technical Reports and certificate applications through it. Dubai Municipality also keeps a unified building database and does periodic assessments. Whether the platform is live yet was not verified. Urbanise sells general FM compliance software for Dubai, and generic inspection apps exist, such as a Process Street Dubai Municipality inspection template. English searches found no product built for Law 3/2026, and the one Arabic search I ran was aimed at building counts and found none either. The core technical work by law belongs to licensed engineering firms, and they cannot delegate it.
result.duty: Dubai Law No. 3 of 2026, issued 27 Feb 2026. It takes effect 60 days after publication in the Official Gazette (Art. 25). I did not confirm the publication date. One secondary source estimated it at about June 2026, which is unverified. Owners must get a Quality and Safety Certificate once 20 years have passed since the building's Completion Certificate (Art. 9). They must appoint a licensed engineering firm to prepare a Technical Report, which is due within 6 months of initial approval (extendable up to 2 years). They must also fix defects through a contractor. The certificate is valid for 10 years if the Completion Certificate is under 40 years old, otherwise 5 years, and is renewable (Art. 13). Buildings under 20 years must do periodic maintenance, by choice or when the authority asks. Owners, contractors and engineering firms have one year from the effective date to comply, extendable once (Art. 22). Fines run from AED 100 to AED 1,000,000, doubled for repeat offences up to AED 2,000,000. The authority can also suspend permits and the attestation of lease contracts (Art. 16). The law applies to free zones including DIFC. The executive resolutions that will set fees, violations and renewal conditions were not reached.
result.market: I found no official count of Dubai buildings aged 20 or more. A 2019 Statista figure (citing Dubai statistics) gives about 72,000 investment villas and 40,600 private villas in Dubai's urban areas, all ages combined. Dubai Municipality licensed about 3,100 to 4,300 new buildings per half-year in 2025 and 2026, but these are new builds and outside the certificate duty for 20 years. The covered stock is probably in the tens of thousands of buildings, mostly older villas and low-rise blocks in older districts (estimate, not verified). Owners need the certificate only once every 5 to 10 years. The number of licensed engineering firms was not found.
result.reason: The duty is real but much narrower than the claim says. Under the official text, only buildings completed 20 or more years ago need a certificate. Newer buildings only owe periodic maintenance when Dubai Municipality asks. The certificate is renewed every 5 to 10 years, so each building faces it rarely, though the one-year compliance window could cause a one-off rush. The licensed engineering firm does the core work: the inspection and the Technical Report. Owners apply and engineering firms file reports through the state's unified Digital Window platform, and the municipality keeps the building database. I found no tailored software, but a tracker adds little value. The obvious buyers are engineering firms, and they are few. Willingness to pay is low.

The duty is real but narrow. Dubai Municipality's food permit service requires prior inspection and approval of home-based businesses before they produce or supply food. Permits need an inspection grade of A, B or C and last one year. Intelaq home licences are reportedly limited to UAE and GCC nationals, and food preparation under Intelaq reportedly needs a separate kitchen outside the home. Eligibility is unclear because the sources are mostly consultancy blogs. FoodWatch is a free DM platform, so no paid niche is evident. Buyers are tiny, inspections come about once a year, and willingness to pay is low. I found no home-baker compliance software, but I only ran two searches, so I did not check this properly. I found no register count of home licences. I found no penalty source beyond unverified consultancy figures. This overlaps the known ideas K04 and K06, so I treat it as a weak variant of them.

Duty is real: Decree-Law 9/2022 (in force 15 Dec 2023) requires the MOHRE unified contract, monthly pay in AED, weekly rest, 30 days' leave and end-of-contract settlement. Violations carry fines up to Dh50,000 (the 153-employer suspension case). Health insurance for domestic workers is employer-paid at residency issue or renewal, in all emirates from 2025. Not confirmed: fine tiers, gratuity rules, and whether WPS is mandatory for households (it was extended via bank and e& apps, and sources say it is at the employer's discretion). Competition: Tadbeer centres, insurers and bank apps already handle visa, insurance and payment. The buyers are B2C households, which are hard to reach with little willingness to pay. Market: roughly 600-750k domestic workers (undated or thesis figures), not an official count. This overlaps rejected K08 and has no revival evidence.

The duty is real. The DoE Tankering Regulation (2020) requires tanker and driver permits and accreditation, tracking devices, tariff filing, and fines of AED 5,000-50,000. But the state already runs the core workflow. The Tankering Management Centre (tmc.fms-tech.com, run by TAQA) registers tankers and drivers, issues accreditation, tracks tankers and handles tariff offers across Abu Dhabi, Al Ain and Al Dhafra. Operators must register through that closed system, so a third-party tool has little left to do. The buyer pool is small and not counted. I could not fetch the ADDC page (403) or confirm whether the regulation has been updated since 2020. Search found no private competitor.

Duty is real: Dubai Municipality requires lifts and escalators to hold an examination and compliance certificate from an accredited body, renewed periodically. The owner or occupier must carry out repairs, and unsafe equipment must be taken out of use and reported (Local Order 11/2003, GU48). Searches did not find the interval, a penalty figure or a filing portal. The GU48 fetch returned nothing useful, so these stayed unchecked. No UAE-specific certificate tracker turned up, only generic lift-maintenance field-service software (Joblogic, Fieldproxy and similar). Weak points: the market is small because most lifts sit with large developers and facility-management firms, which already track certificates. Buyers are few and fragmented, and willingness to pay is low. Abu Dhabi and boiler rules were not checked.

Duty is real per DET pages: annual permit renewal, Tourism Dirham entered by the 15th monthly (late fees), AED 10 standard / 15 deluxe per room per night, capped at 30 nights, owners limited to 8 units. Guest reporting is already covered by Chekin and Guesty AutoComply. DET offers auto-renewal, and property managers or PMS platforms advertise automated Tourism Dirham collection. I found no standalone tool for Tourism Dirham calculation or renewal tracking, so a gap exists only for self-managing owners without a PMS. That segment is small, and most owners hand the work to management firms, so willingness to pay is low. Market size was not checked, and I did not search the Abu Dhabi variant. The DET fee schedule and the per-room versus per-bedroom wording conflict across sources.

Duty is real: Dubai RTA requires an occupational permit per delivery rider (training at accredited institutes, medical test, police clearance, annual renewal), a 4-year bike age limit (optional inspection for a 5th year from Feb 2026), lane limits from 1 Nov 2025, and a front plate for company bikes. Enforcement is active (390+ bikes impounded). I found no dedicated permit-tracking product, only generic fleet and telematics vendors such as Uffizio. Weak points: RTA is building its own telematics monitoring, and small fleets mostly serve platforms that manage compliance. Fleet count not found, penalty amounts not verified, and RTA pages were not fetched. Overlaps category 18. The buyer pool is small and price-sensitive.

The duty looks real but I found no official source. The DMCA (now Dubai Maritime Authority under PCFC) approves commercial vessels, requires inspection at registration and renewal, requires a DED trade licence, and requires a skipper licence valid 5 years. All of this comes from consultancy pages. Inspection interval, fees and TDRA VHF terms are unconfirmed, and the sources conflict. The Abu Dhabi-Dubai mutual permit recognition from Jan 2026 is reported only by news sites and aimed at foreign yachts. Competition: generic yacht-management software (Scyllastar, IYC Blue) tracks certificate expiry, and Dubai firms such as CharterClick sell done-for-you compliance management. No UAE-specific tracker found. The market is small, there is no recurring filing, and per-vessel renewals are handled by agents. Operator count was not found.

Duty is real: ECAS/EQM is mandatory for regulated products imported or sold in the UAE. Per SGS (a MoIAT notified body), ECAS lasts about 1 year with annual renewal, EQM 3 years, halal 3 years. Certificates are not transferable and tie to product and facility. MoIAT issued Ministerial Resolution 137 of 2024 on new marks. No tracking software turned up in English or Arabic searches. Notified bodies (SGS, TUV SUD, RACS) handle renewals and probably send their own reminders. Weak points: the buyer is a consultant or PRO, the problem is a simple expiry calendar, willingness to pay is low, and the market size was not found. Not checked: MoIAT portal API, number of importers, and who files.

Duty is real. MOHAP's page says facility licences renew annually, with a late fine of 25% of base fees per 30 days, up to 6 months, then automatic cancellation. Required documents include the Civil Defence certificate, medical-waste agreement, radiation licence if applicable, and price list. The Arabic search found fees of AED 5,000 (general clinic) and 6,000 (specialist clinic). It found no dedicated licence-expiry tracker. The idea is weak because renewal is only one event a year, and a calendar or a clinic-software add-on covers it. Clinics also use licensing consultants (PROs). The market is fragmented across MOHAP, DHA and DoH, and I found no clinic count. Not checked: DHA and DoH renewal rules, and whether clinics must file medical-waste records.
